units.text: PrivateLink enters at layer four, while the Application Load Balancer makes layer-seven routing decisions. Follow the arrows from a consumer’s private interface endpoint to the provider application.
The endpoint on the left sits in the consumer VPC. It connects to the provider’s endpoint service, exposing the service without granting broad network reachability between the VPCs.

Inside the provider VPC, the Network Load Balancer accepts TCP on port four forty-three. Its target group has type A L B, and forwards TCP on the same port. The N L B can provide static addresses per enabled zone.

Now follow the connection to the A L B’s HTTPS listener. That listener handles HTTPS and applies host or path rules to choose the target group. The two healthy app targets represent application capacity behind those rules.

Use both load balancers when you need private or static entry and HTTP routing. They must share a VPC and account. Register one A L B per N L B target group, match the listener port, and remember this hop uses IPv4.
This diagram is about inserting an inspection appliance into a traffic path, not exposing a service. Trace it from the application VPC on the left to the appliance fleet in the inspection VPC.

Start with the application subnet route table. The highlighted entry steers selected traffic to the Gateway Load Balancer endpoint. Creating the endpoint alone does not make existing routes send traffic through it.

The endpoint hands the traffic to Gateway Load Balancer in the inspection VPC. The connection from the load balancer to its appliance target group uses GENEVE over UDP port six thousand eighty-one, preserving the original packet inside the encapsulation.

The healthy third-party appliance on the right inspects the traffic and returns permitted packets to the load balancer. The appliance applies the inspection policy. The load balancer distributes flows; it does not make the firewall decision.
Validate forward and reverse routing through inspection. If the return side bypasses the appliance, an apparently correct outbound route is not enough for a stateful firewall.
This slide explains why the two traffic directions need the same appliance: the appliance tracks connection state. The colored paths distinguish two separate flows, not two individual packets.

On the left, both Flow A and Flow B arrive at the Gateway Load Balancer. Think of them as independent conversations. Sending packets from one conversation to different appliances can split the state needed to recognize replies.

In the middle, the load balancer assigns each example flow to a healthy appliance when it starts. Flow A goes to Appliance A, while Flow B goes to Appliance B. The decision is per flow, not round-robin per packet.

On the right, the response from Flow A needs to reach Appliance A again, and likewise for Flow B. Don’t interpret this illustration as automatic session recovery: by default, established flows may stay with a target even if it becomes unhealthy.

The design check is symmetric routing. Trace both directions to the inspection path and verify the appliance sees each half of the conversation. The GENEVE label describes the load-balancer-to-appliance traffic, not a new client protocol.
